about: The scripted AI lesson for p4-radioactivity (2026-11-27, Phase C, brief docs/briefs/2026-11-27-phase-c-physics.md): every word she sees is written here once and checked (tools/check-script.js, tools/review-lesson.js --script). The AI only marks her typed answers (choosing a branch written here), answers her own questions, and sorts her messages. It opens with two recall questions from p4-nuclear-model.

steps.text: Welcome! This lesson is about the radiation that comes out of the nucleus, the tiny centre, of some atoms: what it is, what stops it, and where it comes from.

steps.question: First, two quick questions from the last lesson. What is in the nucleus of an atom?
steps.right: Yes: protons and neutrons are in the nucleus; electrons are outside it.

wrong.other: Not quite: protons and neutrons.
wrong.electrons: Not quite: electrons are outside the nucleus. The nucleus holds protons and neutrons.
wrong.only: Not quite: electrons are outside the nucleus. The nucleus holds protons and neutrons.

idk.hint: Electrons are outside the nucleus. The other two particles are inside it.

steps.answerWhy: The nucleus holds protons and neutrons; electrons are outside it.

steps.question: Second: what does the atomic number of an atom count?
steps.right: Yes: the atomic number counts the protons, and it decides the element. The mass number counts protons plus neutrons.

wrong.other: Not quite: its protons.
wrong.both: Not quite: protons plus neutrons is the mass number. The atomic number counts the protons only.
wrong.neutrons: Not quite: the atomic number counts the protons, and it decides the element.

idk.hint: The atomic number decides the element, and that is set by the protons.

steps.answerWhy: The atomic number is the number of protons, which decides the element.

steps.text: Now this lesson. Some nuclei are unstable: they cannot stay as they are forever.
Radiation is energy or particles given out by something. Here it means what comes out of a nucleus.
An unstable nucleus gives out radiation as it changes to become more stable. This is called radioactive decay.
Radioactive decay is random: you cannot predict which nucleus will decay next, or when.

steps.question: Two identical unstable nuclei sit side by side. Which one will decay first?
steps.right: Yes: decay is random, so no one can tell which will go first.

wrong.other: Not quite: no one can tell.
wrong.left: Not quite: position makes no difference. Decay is random, so no one can tell which goes first.
wrong.same: Not quite: being identical does not make them decay together. Decay is random, so no one can tell which goes first.

idk.hint: Random means it cannot be predicted.

steps.answerWhy: Radioactive decay is random, so you cannot tell which nucleus will decay first.

steps.text: A radioactive source is a piece of material containing unstable nuclei.
The activity of a source is the number of its nuclei that decay each second.
Activity is measured in becquerels (Bq). 1 Bq is one decay each second.

steps.question: A source has an activity of 300 Bq. What does that mean?
steps.right: Yes: 300 decays every second.

wrong.other: Not quite: 300 nuclei decay each second.
wrong.number: Not quite: activity is not how many nuclei there are. It is how many decay each second: 300.
wrong.time: Not quite: activity is a rate, not a time. 300 Bq means 300 nuclei decay each second.

idk.hint: 1 Bq is one decay each second, so 300 Bq is 300 of them each second.

steps.answerWhy: An activity of 300 Bq means 300 nuclei decay each second.

steps.text: A detector is a device that senses radiation. A Geiger-Muller tube is a detector that clicks for each bit of radiation that reaches it.
The number of clicks each second is the count rate. It is less than the activity, because radiation goes out in all directions and the tube only catches some of it.
The radiation from a nucleus comes in a few kinds. This lesson takes three of them in turn, starting with alpha.
An alpha particle (α) is 2 protons and 2 neutrons stuck together: the same as the nucleus of a helium atom.
When a nucleus gives out an alpha particle, it loses 2 protons and 2 neutrons.
The nucleus's mass number, protons plus neutrons, falls by 4. Its atomic number falls by 2. A different atomic number means a different element.

steps.question: A nucleus with mass number 226 gives out an alpha particle. What is the mass number of the new nucleus?
steps.right: Yes: 222. It loses 2 protons and 2 neutrons, so 226 − 4 = 222.

wrong.other: Not quite: 222. The mass number falls by 4: 226 − 4 = 222.
wrong.two: Not quite: 222. An alpha particle holds 2 protons and 2 neutrons, so the mass number falls by 4: 226 − 4 = 222.
wrong.add: Not quite: 222. The nucleus loses the alpha particle, so take 4 away: 226 − 4 = 222.

idk.hint: An alpha particle holds 4 particles: 2 protons and 2 neutrons. Take 4 away from 226.

steps.answerWhy: An alpha particle has a mass number of 4, so the new mass number is 226 − 4 = 222.

steps.text: An ion is an atom that has lost or gained electrons.
Radiation that knocks electrons off atoms as it passes, making ions, is called ionising radiation. It is harmful because it damages the cells of the body.
Alpha is highly ionising: each alpha particle makes lots of ions.
Making all those ions uses up an alpha particle's energy fast. So alpha only travels about 5 cm in air, and a sheet of paper stops it.

steps.question: A smoke alarm holds a tiny alpha source. Why is it safe to have one on the ceiling?

options.text: It only gives out radiation when there is smoke
Alpha only travels a few cm in air

steps.right: Yes: alpha only travels a few cm in air, so it never reaches the people below.

wrong.other: Not quite: alpha only travels a few cm in air.
wrong.notion: Not quite: alpha is highly ionising. It is safe because alpha only travels a few cm in air, so it never reaches you.
wrong.smoke: Not quite: radioactive decay never stops. It is safe because alpha only travels a few cm in air, so it never reaches you.

idk.hint: The ceiling is more than a metre above you. Think about how far alpha travels.

steps.answerWhy: Alpha only travels about 5 cm in air, so an alpha source on the ceiling cannot reach you.

steps.text: Outside the body, skin stops alpha. But breathed in or swallowed, an alpha source is very dangerous: nothing shields the cells, and alpha ionises so much.

steps.prompt: In one line: what is an alpha particle, and what stops it?
points: an alpha particle is 2 protons and 2 neutrons
a sheet of paper stops it
steps.idk: No problem. A good line would be: an alpha particle is 2 protons and 2 neutrons, like a helium nucleus, and a sheet of paper stops it.

steps.text: The second kind of radiation is beta (β). A beta particle is a fast-moving electron given out by the nucleus.
Where does an electron in the nucleus come from? A neutron turns into a proton and an electron. The new electron shoots out as the beta particle; the proton stays behind.
In beta decay, one neutron is lost and one proton is gained. The number of protons plus neutrons, the mass number, stays the same. The atomic number goes up by 1.

steps.question: Carbon-14 has atomic number 6. It gives out a beta particle. What is the atomic number of the new nucleus?
steps.right: Yes: 7. A neutron became a proton, so 6 + 1 = 7. Atomic number 7 is nitrogen.

wrong.other: Not quite: 7. The atomic number goes up by 1.
wrong.down: Not quite: in beta decay a neutron turns into a proton, so the nucleus gains a proton: 6 + 1 = 7.
wrong.same: Not quite: the mass number stays the same, but the atomic number goes up by 1, because a neutron became a proton: 7.

idk.hint: In beta decay, a neutron turns into a proton, so the number of protons goes up.

steps.answerWhy: A neutron turns into a proton, so the atomic number goes up by 1: 6 + 1 = 7.

steps.text: Beta is less ionising than alpha. So it keeps its energy for longer and travels further: about 1 m in air.
Paper does not stop beta. A sheet of aluminium a few millimetres thick does.

steps.question: Radiation from a source gets through paper but not through a few mm of aluminium. Which kind is it?
steps.right: Yes: paper stops alpha, so radiation that gets through paper but not aluminium is beta.

wrong.other: Not quite: beta.
wrong.alpha: Not quite: paper stops alpha, so alpha could not get through it. Getting through paper but not aluminium is beta.
wrong.either: Not quite: alpha cannot get through paper at all. Getting through paper but not aluminium is beta.

idk.hint: Paper stops alpha. This radiation got through the paper.

steps.answerWhy: Paper stops alpha, so radiation that passes paper but is stopped by aluminium is beta.

steps.prompt: In one line: how does a nucleus change when it gives out a beta particle?
points: a neutron turns into a proton (and an electron)
the atomic number goes up by 1 and the mass number stays the same
steps.idk: No problem. A good line would be: in beta decay a neutron turns into a proton, so the atomic number goes up by 1 and the mass number stays the same.

steps.text: The third kind is gamma. Gamma rays (γ) are not particles but waves of energy, like light, with far more energy.
Waves of energy that travel like light are called electromagnetic radiation. Radio waves and X-rays are other kinds. Gamma rays come from a nucleus.
Gamma rays have no mass and no charge.
A nucleus that gives out gamma keeps the same mass number and atomic number. Gamma often comes out just after an alpha or beta decay.
Gamma is weakly ionising: it makes few ions, so it travels a long way through air and through the body. Thick lead or thick concrete reduces it a lot, but never stops it completely.

steps.question: A detector picks up radiation that has come through a few millimetres of aluminium. Which kind is it?
steps.right: Yes: aluminium stops alpha and beta, so only gamma gets through.

wrong.other: Not quite: gamma.
wrong.beta: Not quite: a few mm of aluminium stops beta. Only gamma gets through.
wrong.alpha: Not quite: paper stops alpha, so it could never get through aluminium. Only gamma does.

idk.hint: Paper stops alpha, and a few mm of aluminium stop beta. Only one kind is left.

steps.answerWhy: Aluminium stops alpha and beta, so radiation that gets through it is gamma.

steps.text: The picture puts all three side by side: alpha ends at the paper, beta ends at the aluminium, and some gamma still gets through the lead.
To penetrate means to get through something. To choose radiation for a job, compare how far each kind penetrates, its range in air and how strongly it ionises.
For example, doctors can put a source inside a patient to see an organ. Its radiation must get out to a detector outside the body, so they use gamma: alpha and beta would be absorbed inside the body.

steps.question: Which radiation is the most strongly ionising?
steps.right: Yes: alpha is the most ionising, then beta, then gamma.

wrong.other: Not quite: alpha.
wrong.gamma: Not quite: gamma is the least ionising, which is why it travels so far. Alpha is the most ionising.
wrong.beta: Not quite: beta is in the middle. Alpha is the most ionising, which is why it is stopped so easily.

idk.hint: The kind stopped most easily uses up its energy fastest, making ions. Paper stops one of them.

steps.answerWhy: Alpha is the most ionising, then beta, then gamma.

steps.prompt: In one line: what is gamma radiation, and what does lead do to it?
points: gamma is electromagnetic radiation (waves from the nucleus)
thick lead reduces it but does not stop it completely
steps.idk: No problem. A good line would be: gamma is electromagnetic radiation from the nucleus, and thick lead reduces it but never stops it completely.

steps.text: Radiation is around us all the time, at a low level. This is called background radiation. Some of it comes from nature, and some is man-made: made by people.
The biggest natural source in the UK is radon: a radioactive gas that seeps out of some rocks.
Another natural source is cosmic rays: radiation from space. Rocks, buildings, food and drink add a little more.
Fallout is radioactive dust that spreads through the air after a nuclear explosion or accident, then slowly settles.
Man-made sources include medical X-rays, fallout from nuclear weapons tests, and nuclear accidents.

steps.question: Which of these is a natural source of background radiation?
steps.right: Yes: radon comes out of rocks, so it is natural.

wrong.other: Not quite: radon gas from rocks.
wrong.xray: Not quite: X-rays are made by machines in hospitals, so they are man-made. Radon gas comes from rocks: natural.
wrong.accident: Not quite: an accident at a nuclear power station is man-made. Radon gas comes from rocks: natural.

idk.hint: One of these would exist even if people had never built anything.

steps.answerWhy: Radon gas from rocks is natural; X-rays and nuclear accidents are man-made.

steps.text: How much radiation a person receives is called their dose.
Dose is measured in sieverts (Sv). A smaller unit is the millisievert (mSv): 1000 mSv = 1 Sv.

steps.question: Two people live in different parts of the UK. Why might one of them get a bigger background dose?

options.text: More radon comes out of the rocks where they live

steps.right: Yes: some rocks give out more radon than others. Your job matters too: working with X-rays adds to your dose.

wrong.other: Not quite: more radon comes out of the rocks where they live.
wrong.people: Not quite: other people do not give out radiation. Some rocks give out more radon, so where you live matters.
wrong.electric: Not quite: using electricity does not add radiation. Some rocks give out more radon, so where you live matters.

idk.hint: The biggest natural source comes out of rocks, and rocks differ from place to place.

steps.answerWhy: Some rocks give out more radon than others, so your background dose depends on where you live.

steps.text: Now the numbers in decay. In a symbol like ²²⁶₈₈Ra, Ra is the element (radium). The top number is the mass number and the bottom number is the atomic number.
An alpha particle is written ⁴₂He: mass number 4 and atomic number 2, the same as a helium nucleus.
Radium-226 gives out an alpha particle and becomes radon-222: ²²⁶₈₈Ra → ²²²₈₆Rn + ⁴₂He. The arrow means "becomes". A decay written with symbols like this is called a nuclear equation.
In a nuclear equation the top numbers add up to the same on each side: 226 = 222 + 4. The bottom numbers do too: 88 = 86 + 2.

steps.question: Now radon-222, ²²²₈₆Rn, decays in the same way. What is the atomic number of the nucleus it becomes?
steps.right: Yes: 84. The alpha particle takes 2 protons: 86 − 2 = 84.

wrong.other: Not quite: 84. 86 − 2 = 84.
wrong.add: Not quite: 84. The nucleus loses the alpha particle, so take 2 away: 86 − 2 = 84.
wrong.four: Not quite: 84. Take 2 off the atomic number (the 2 protons) and 4 off the mass number: 86 − 2 = 84.
wrong.mass: Not quite: 84. 218 is the new mass number, 222 − 4. The atomic number is 86 − 2 = 84.

idk.hint: An alpha particle is ⁴₂He. Take its bottom number, 2, away from 86.

steps.answerWhy: An alpha particle has atomic number 2, so the new atomic number is 86 − 2 = 84.

steps.text: A beta particle is written ⁰₋₁e. Its mass is so small that its top number is 0. Its bottom number is −1, which keeps the bottom numbers balanced when a neutron turns into a proton.
Carbon-14 gives out a beta particle and becomes nitrogen-14: ¹⁴₆C → ¹⁴₇N + ⁰₋₁e. Top: 14 = 14 + 0. Bottom: 6 = 7 + (−1).

steps.question: Potassium-40, ⁴⁰₁₉K, gives out a beta particle. Ca is calcium, Cl is chlorine and Ar is argon. Which is the new nucleus?
steps.right: Yes: ⁴⁰₂₀Ca. Top: 40 = 40 + 0. Bottom: 19 = 20 + (−1).

wrong.other: Not quite: ⁴⁰₂₀Ca.
wrong.alpha: Not quite: that is what alpha decay would give. In beta decay the top number stays 40 and the bottom goes up by 1: ⁴⁰₂₀Ca.
wrong.down: Not quite: the atomic number goes up in beta decay, not down: 19 + 1 = 20, so ⁴⁰₂₀Ca.

idk.hint: In beta decay the top number stays the same and the bottom number goes up by 1.

steps.answerWhy: Beta decay keeps the mass number at 40 and raises the atomic number to 20: ⁴⁰₂₀Ca.

steps.prompt: In one line: what must be true of the numbers in a nuclear equation?
points: the top numbers (mass numbers) add up the same on each side
the bottom numbers (atomic numbers) add up the same on each side
steps.idk: No problem. A good line would be: in a nuclear equation, the mass numbers on each side add up to the same total, and so do the atomic numbers.

steps.text: Now for a short quiz: six questions on the whole lesson. Take your time.

steps.question: Quiz, question 1 of 6: what is an alpha particle made of?

options.text: A helium atom with its electrons

steps.right: Yes: 2 protons and 2 neutrons, a helium nucleus.

wrong.other: Not quite: 2 protons and 2 neutrons.
wrong.w1: Not quite: that is a beta particle. An alpha particle is 2 protons and 2 neutrons.
wrong.w2: Not quite: it has no electrons: it is a helium nucleus, 2 protons and 2 neutrons.

steps.answerWhy: An alpha particle is 2 protons and 2 neutrons: a helium nucleus.

steps.question: Quiz, question 2 of 6: which radiation is stopped by a sheet of paper?
steps.right: Yes: paper stops alpha.

wrong.other: Not quite: alpha.
wrong.w1: Not quite: beta needs a few mm of aluminium. Paper stops alpha.
wrong.w2: Not quite: gamma is only reduced, by thick lead. Paper stops alpha.

steps.answerWhy: Alpha is stopped by a sheet of paper.

steps.question: Quiz, question 3 of 6: in beta decay, what happens to the mass number?
steps.right: Yes: it stays the same; the atomic number goes up by 1.

wrong.other: Not quite: it stays the same.
wrong.w1: Not quite: that is alpha decay. In beta decay a neutron becomes a proton, so the mass number stays the same.
wrong.w2: Not quite: the atomic number goes up by 1. The mass number stays the same.

steps.answerWhy: A neutron turns into a proton, so the mass number stays the same and the atomic number goes up by 1.

steps.question: Quiz, question 4 of 6: which is a man-made source of background radiation?
steps.right: Yes: X-rays are made by machines.

wrong.other: Not quite: medical X-rays.
wrong.w1: Not quite: cosmic rays come from space: natural. Medical X-rays are man-made.
wrong.w2: Not quite: radon comes from rocks: natural. Medical X-rays are man-made.

steps.answerWhy: Medical X-rays are man-made; cosmic rays and radon are natural.

steps.question: Quiz, question 5 of 6: a nucleus gives out a gamma ray. What happens to its atomic number?
steps.right: Yes: gamma has no mass and no charge, so both numbers stay the same.

wrong.other: Not quite: it stays the same.
wrong.w1: Not quite: that is alpha decay. Gamma has no mass and no charge, so the atomic number stays the same.
wrong.w2: Not quite: that is beta decay. Gamma has no mass and no charge, so the atomic number stays the same.

steps.answerWhy: Gamma has no mass and no charge, so the atomic number and mass number stay the same.

steps.question: Quiz, question 6 of 6: polonium-210, ²¹⁰₈₄Po, gives out an alpha particle. What is the mass number of the new nucleus?

wrong.other: Not quite: 206. An alpha particle takes away mass number 4: 210 − 4 = 206.

steps.answerWhy: An alpha particle has mass number 4, so the new mass number is 210 − 4 = 206.
